q: What block level is needed for third-degree tear repair under spinal?
why: Sacral cover is essential; T10 is enough.

q: What is a common complication after spinal for perineal repair?
why: Bladder care is essential after neuraxial block.

q: Which nerve carries second stage and perineal pain?
why: The pudendal nerve is less well covered by a lumbar epidural alone.

q: What is bupivacaine’s main advantage over lidocaine for labour epidural infusions?
o: No motor block at any dose
why: Lidocaine shows tachyphylaxis; ropivacaine has an improved safety profile with lower potency.

q: Which intrathecal opioid has the greatest CSF spread and risk of delayed respiratory depression?
why: Morphine has low lipid solubility, spreads further in CSF and has a higher risk of delayed respiratory depression.

q: What is the occupational exposure limit for nitrous oxide?
why: Keep exposure under 100 ppm; Entonox is 50:50 N2O and oxygen.

q: Which component of a tear defines third-degree?
o: Involvement of the anal sphincter complex
why: Third-degree tears involve the anal sphincter; fourth-degree also involve the rectal mucosa.

q: What skin prep is used for neuraxial procedures?
why: Use 0.5% chlorhexidine in alcohol, allowed to dry, to limit neurotoxicity risk.

q: After delivery, how long does raised aspiration risk persist?
why: Reflux and delayed emptying persist for at least 24–48 hours; use aspiration prophylaxis.
